question_text: Integer keys are inserted, in this order, into an empty hash table with 7 slots (indexes 0 to 6), using the hashing function h(k) = k mod 7: 15, 22, 8, 29, 3. (i) Using linear probing, state the index at which each key is stored. (ii) Calculate the load factor after all five insertions. (iii) Instead, using separate chaining, state the contents of each non-empty slot. (iv) Explain why many implementations enlarge the table when the load factor exceeds a threshold such as 0.7.
adaptation_rationale: Original question written by Claude (single-agent Chunk 3 continuation, 2026-11-04) for a syllabus statement with no linked question at handover; no historical source question or official marking status claimed.
solution: (i) 15 -> 1; 22 -> 2 (1 occupied); 8 -> 3 (1, 2 occupied); 29 -> 4 (1, 2, 3 occupied); 3 -> 5 (3, 4 occupied). (ii) 5 / 7 = 0.71 (approximately). (iii) Slot 1: 15, 22, 8, 29 (in insertion order); slot 3: 3. (iv) As the load factor rises, collisions become more frequent, so probe sequences / chains become longer and insertion and lookup slow down from about O(1) towards O(n); enlarging the table and rehashing keeps the load factor low so operations stay close to constant time.

marking_points.criterion: (iv) higher load factor means more collisions/longer probes or chains, so slower operations; resizing restores near O(1).

acceptable_alternatives: Follow-through for later keys in (i) from one earlier placement error. Accept chain order shown as most-recent-first if stated.
partial_credit_notes: Award each independent point once, up to 6 marks. Accept equivalent correct wording or valid alternative code. Do not double-credit one idea.

verification.scope: Integer keys only; string hashing is constructed in O-C3-B-008.
